subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: C'(150) = 2.7 is just a number until you can say what it MEANS: at a production level of 150 units, cost is rising about $2.70 per additional unit. The AP dedicates entire rubric points to that sentence — this chapter teaches you to write it every time.
learning_objectives: Interpret f'(a) in context with correct units and a complete sentence
Construct derivative units as output units per input unit
Distinguish the meanings of f(a), f'(a), and changes Δf in applied settings
Translate prose descriptions of rates into derivative statements and back
Use f'(a) to estimate nearby function values and changes

sections.title: The Interpretation Sentence
sections.subtitle: Four ingredients, every time
sections.body:
A complete interpretation of f'(a) names four things: WHAT quantity is changing (the output), WITH RESPECT TO what (the input), the VALUE with UNITS, and WHERE/WHEN it applies (at the specific input a). Template: 'At [a, input units], [the output quantity] is increasing/decreasing at a rate of [|value|, output units per input unit].'

Example: W(t) is the weight of a puppy in pounds at age t weeks, and W'(8) = 1.5. Interpretation: 'At age 8 weeks, the puppy's weight is increasing at a rate of 1.5 pounds per week.' All four ingredients present. Compare the zero-credit versions: 'the weight changes by 1.5' (no when, no units, no direction), 'the derivative is 1.5 pounds per week' (no when, restates notation without meaning).

Sign handling: for negative derivatives, say DECREASING with the positive magnitude — H'(3) = -40 reads 'at t = 3, the altitude is decreasing at 40 feet per minute,' not 'increasing at -40.' Graders accept either mathematically, but the decreasing-phrasing demonstrates the understanding being tested and never backfires.

The sentence is genuinely graded: AP rubrics for interpretation parts allocate the point for units AND the 'at a' reference AND the direction. Practice until the template is automatic — it is the cheapest reliable point on the entire exam.
key_terms: At [input value], [output] is increasing/decreasing at [magnitude, output-per-input units]
What changes, with respect to what, value with units, where/when
Negative rates read as 'decreasing at [positive magnitude]'
boxes: ap_alert

The rubric language for interpretation points is unforgiving about 'at': f'(8) describes the instant t = 8, not 'around week 8' or 'during the first 8 weeks.' Anchor every interpretation to the exact input value.

sections.title: Units Arithmetic
sections.subtitle: Output per input, mechanically
sections.body:
Derivative units are a fraction: the output's units over the input's units. R(t) in gallons, t in hours: R' in gallons per hour. P(x) in dollars, x in items: P' in dollars per item. No memorization — read the function's units, read the input's units, divide.

Second derivatives stack the input units twice: R'' in gallons per hour per hour (gallons/hour²). The prose meaning — 'the rate at which the flow rate changes' — sounds stilted precisely because it is two layers deep; trust the units arithmetic over linguistic intuition.

Composite contexts demand care about WHICH variables the derivative connects. If C(g) is the cost in dollars of g gallons, and g(t) is gallons consumed by time t hours, then C'(g) carries dollars per gallon, g'(t) carries gallons per hour, and the chain rule product dC/dt = C'(g(t))·g'(t) carries dollars per hour — units multiplying and canceling exactly like the derivatives do. Unit consistency is a built-in chain rule audit.

Dimensionless inputs or outputs exist: if E(p) is efficiency (a pure percent) as a function of pressure p in psi, E' carries 'percent per psi.' And inverse functions invert units (Unit 3's observation): if f maps hours to miles, f⁻¹ maps miles to hours and its derivative carries hours per mile. Units are calculus's accounting system — keep the books and entire problem classes self-verify.
key_terms: Derivative units = output units / input units, always
f'' units divide by the input units twice: per hour per hour
boxes: ap_alert

When an FRQ asks for 'units of f''(3)' — and it does, by name — the answer is mechanical: output per input per input. Writing gallons/hour² (or gallons per hour per hour) collects the point; describing the meaning without the units does not.

sections.title: Value, Rate, and Change
sections.subtitle: f(a), f'(a), and Δf are three different numbers
sections.body:
Three quantities coexist in every applied problem and answer three different questions. f(a): how much IS there at a (a level). f'(a): how fast is it changing at a (a rate). Δf = f(b) - f(a): how much did it change between a and b (an accumulation). Exam questions specify which one they want with precise phrasing, and matching phrase to quantity is the skill.

Phrase decoder: 'how much water is in the tank at t = 3' → f(3). 'How fast is water entering at t = 3' → f'(3). 'How much water entered between t = 1 and t = 3' → f(3) - f(1). 'Average rate of inflow over [1, 3]' → (f(3) - f(1))/2. The decoder matters most under pressure, when 'how fast' and 'how much' blur.

A level and its rate are independent: a tank can be nearly full (large f) while draining (negative f'), or nearly empty while filling fast. Exam traps exploit the confusion — 'the population is large, so it must be growing' is a non sequitur the questions are built to catch.

The rate-to-change bridge: over a SHORT interval, change ≈ rate × time: Δf ≈ f'(a)·Δt. The puppy gaining 1.5 lb/week at week 8 gains roughly 0.75 lb in the next half week. This approximation — the tangent line in disguise — is the next section's star, and eventually (Unit 6) integration makes it exact: total change is the integral of the rate.
key_terms: f(a) is an amount, f'(a) a speed of change, Δf an accumulated difference
'How much at' → value; 'how fast' → derivative; 'how much between' → difference
Δf ≈ f'(a)Δt — rate times time approximates change nearby
boxes: ap_alert
'Is the amount of water increasing or decreasing at t = 5?' is answered by the SIGN of f'(5) alone — not by comparing f(5) to f(4), and not by f(5)'s size. One sign, one sentence, full credit.

sections.title: Estimation with the Derivative
sections.subtitle: The tangent line goes applied
sections.body:
The derivative's estimation power: f(a + h) ≈ f(a) + f'(a)·h for small h. It is the tangent line from Unit 2 wearing applied clothes — start at the known value, move along the known slope. If the population is 4,500 at year 10 growing at 120 per year, the year-12 estimate is 4,500 + 120(2) = 4,740.

Table problems combine this with Unit 2's secant estimates: given a table of f values, estimate f'(a) by a straddling difference quotient, THEN extrapolate with it. Two estimates stacked — the exam grades the setup of each, so show the difference quotient and the tangent-line arithmetic as separate steps.

How good is the estimate? It depends on h (smaller is better) and on how curved f is (straighter is better). The error direction is predictable when concavity is known: tangent lines sit BELOW concave-up curves (underestimates) and ABOVE concave-down curves (overestimates). The full theory arrives with linearization in Chapter 6 of this unit; plant the geometric picture now.

Estimates deserve estimate language: 'approximately,' '≈,' 'about.' Claiming exact equality from a tangent-line extrapolation is a half-point error in interpretation parts. Calibrated honesty — exact when exact, approximate when approximate — is both good mathematics and good rubric strategy.
key_terms: f(a + h) ≈ f(a) + f'(a)h — known value plus slope times step
Secant slope from a table feeds the tangent-line extrapolation
Concave up: tangent underestimates; concave down: overestimates
boxes: ap_alert

Estimation FRQs grade three visible steps: the derivative estimate (with the quotient shown), the tangent-line arithmetic, and the 'approximately' in the final sentence. Three steps, three marks — compress them and marks evaporate.

mcq.question: V(t) gives the volume of water in a reservoir in acre-feet, t in days. The units of V''(t) are
mcq.explanation: Second derivatives divide by the input units twice: acre-feet/day².

mcq.question: T(m) is the temperature in °C of a patient m minutes after taking medication, with T(30) = 38.2 and T'(30) = -0.06. The best interpretation of T'(30) is:

choices.B: at 30 minutes, the temperature is falling at 0.06°C per minute
choices.D: the temperature falls 0.06°C every minute thereafter

mcq.explanation: Rate, at the instant m = 30, decreasing, with units. A interprets T(30); C is a change; D wrongly extends the instantaneous rate forever.

mcq.question: A bacteria colony has P(5) = 2,000 and P'(5) = 150 (organisms per hour). The tangent-line estimate of P(5.4) is
G(t) is gasoline in a tank (gallons) at time t (minutes). Which question is answered by G(10) - G(4)?

choices.A: How fast is gasoline leaving at t = 7?
choices.B: How much gasoline is in the tank at t = 10?
choices.C: What is the net change in gasoline from t = 4 to t = 10?
choices.D: What is the average amount of gasoline over [4, 10]?

mcq.explanation: A difference of values is an accumulated net change. A wants a derivative; B a single value; D an average of values, not a difference.

mcq.question: If f is concave down near a, the tangent-line estimate of f(a + h) for small h > 0 is
mcq.explanation: Concave-down curves bend below their tangent lines, so the line sits above the curve: overestimate.

frq.question:
The depth of water in a harbor is D(t) meters, t hours after midnight. Selected values: D(0) = 8.1, D(2) = 9.4, D(4) = 9.8, D(6) = 8.9, D(8) = 7.6.
(a) Estimate D'(5) using the best available difference quotient. Show your work.
(b) Interpret your answer to (a) in a complete sentence with units.
(c) Using D(4) and your estimate of the rate at t = 5 applied from t = 4, estimate the depth at t = 4.5, and state whether your answer is exact.
rubric: (b) Sentence: at 5 hours after midnight, the depth is decreasing at approximately 0.45 meters per hour
States the result is an approximation (secant standing in for tangent; tangent standing in for curve)
frq.model_answer: (a) The smallest interval containing t = 5 is [4, 6]: D'(5) ≈ (8.9 - 9.8)/2 = -0.45. (b) At 5 hours after midnight, the harbor's depth is decreasing at approximately 0.45 meters per hour. (c) D(4.5) ≈ D(4) + (-0.45)(0.5) = 9.8 - 0.225 = 9.575 m. Not exact: the rate is itself a table estimate, and the tangent-line step assumes the depth changes linearly over the half hour — both are approximations.

frq.question:
A company's profit is P(x) thousand dollars when x hundred units are produced. It is known that P(12) = 350 and P'(12) = -15.
(a) Interpret P'(12) in context.
(b) The CEO argues: 'Profit is 350 thousand dollars — production level 12 is clearly working.' Use the distinction between a value and a rate to critique the argument.
(c) Estimate the production level change needed to restore profit growth if P''(12) = 5 (thousand dollars per hundred-units squared), assuming P' changes at roughly that constant rate.
rubric: (a) At a production level of 1200 units, profit is decreasing at about 15 thousand dollars per additional hundred units
(b) The level P(12) = 350 is high, but the rate P'(12) < 0 means the position is eroding — value and rate are independent
(c) Need P' to rise from -15 to 0 at ~5 per unit of x: Δx ≈ 15/5 = 3 hundred units
Frames the answer as an estimate based on the constant-rate assumption
frq.model_answer: (a) When the company produces 1,200 units (x = 12), profit is decreasing at a rate of approximately 15 thousand dollars per additional hundred units produced. (b) The CEO cites a level; the trouble is the rate. P(12) = 350 says the company is currently profitable, but P'(12) = -15 says each additional unit of production is shrinking that profit — a high value with a negative rate is a peak being descended, not a strategy working. (c) P' must climb from -15 to 0. If P' rises at about P''(12) = 5 per hundred-units, the required change is Δx ≈ 15/5 = 3 — roughly 300 units of production adjustment (an estimate, assuming P'' stays near 5).

frq.question:
The function R(t) gives the rate, in liters per minute, at which a pump fills a tank at time t minutes. (Note carefully: R is already a RATE.)
(a) What are the units of R'(t), and what does R'(2) = 3 mean in context?
(b) A student interprets R(5) = 40 as 'the tank contains 40 liters at t = 5.' Explain the error and give the correct interpretation.
(c) Write an expression (using values of R, not an integral) that would APPROXIMATE the amount of water added from t = 5 to t = 5.2, and compute it using R(5) = 40.
rubric: (a) Liters per minute per minute; at t = 2, the pumping rate is increasing by 3 L/min each minute
(b) R(5) is a rate, not an amount: at t = 5 water enters at 40 L/min; the tank's contents are not given
(c) Amount ≈ R(5)·Δt = 40 × 0.2 = 8 liters
Approximation language used (rate treated as constant over the short interval)
frq.model_answer: (a) R' carries liters per minute per minute (L/min²). R'(2) = 3 means: at t = 2 minutes, the pump's filling RATE is increasing at 3 liters-per-minute each minute — the pump is ramping up. (b) The student confused a rate with a level. R(5) = 40 says water is ENTERING at 40 liters per minute at the instant t = 5; it says nothing about how much water has accumulated. (c) Over a short interval, change ≈ rate × time: water added ≈ R(5) × 0.2 = 40 × 0.2 = 8 liters, approximately — exact accumulation would require integrating R, which Unit 6 makes precise.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: One particle, one number line, three functions: where it is, how fast it moves, how its speed changes. Particle motion is the AP's favorite stage for derivatives — every concept from four units performs here, and the vocabulary is graded word by word.
learning_objectives: Relate position, velocity, and acceleration via s' = v and v' = a
Determine direction of motion and rest moments from velocity's sign
Distinguish speed from velocity and analyze speeding up versus slowing down
Compute displacement and total distance over an interval from position
Translate motion vocabulary into precise calculus conditions

sections.title: The Kinematic Chain
sections.subtitle: s, v, a and the dictionary
sections.body:
Position s(t) locates the particle on its line at time t — signed, with a chosen origin and positive direction. Velocity v(t) = s'(t) is the rate position changes: positive means rightward (or upward — match the problem's convention), negative leftward, zero momentarily at rest. Acceleration a(t) = v'(t) = s''(t) is the rate velocity changes.

The core dictionary, graded verbatim on FRQs: 'at rest' ⟺ v(t) = 0. 'Moving right' ⟺ v(t) > 0. 'Changes direction' ⟺ v changes SIGN (not merely v = 0 — the sign must actually flip across the time). 'Velocity is increasing' ⟺ a(t) > 0. Each phrase is a precise equation or inequality; motion FRQs are translation tests.

The v = 0 subtlety deserves its own paragraph: a particle with v(2) = 0 but v > 0 on both sides (like v(t) = (t-2)^2) pauses without turning. Direction change requires a sign change, exactly like Unit 5's coming distinction between critical points and actual extrema. The parallel is not coincidence — v's sign chart IS a derivative sign chart.

Worked spine for the chapter: s(t) = t^3 - 9t^2 + 24t, so v(t) = 3t^2 - 18t + 24 = 3(t-2)(t-4) and a(t) = 6t - 18. Rest at t = 2, 4. Sign chart for v: positive, negative, positive on (0,2), (2,4), (4,∞) — rightward, turn, leftward, turn, rightward. Every subsequent section interrogates this particle further.
key_terms: s' = v, v' = a: each level is the previous one's rate
v(t) = 0 — the exact translation, nothing about a or s
v changes sign (zero with an actual flip), not merely v = 0
boxes: ap_alert

'Does the particle change direction at t = 2?' requires checking v's sign on BOTH sides of 2, and the rubric wants both signs named: 'v > 0 on (0,2) and v < 0 on (2,4), so yes.' Citing v(2) = 0 alone is the incomplete answer the question is designed to catch.

sections.title: Speed Is Not Velocity
sections.subtitle: |v| and the speeding-up test
sections.body:
Speed is the magnitude of velocity: speed = |v(t)|. A particle with v = -5 moves at speed 5 — fast, leftward. Velocity carries direction; speed does not. The distinction powers the unit's most-tested question: is the particle speeding up or slowing down?

The test: speed increases when v and a share a sign, decreases when they oppose. Reasoning: a > 0 pushes velocity upward — which increases |v| if v is already positive, but drags a negative v toward zero (braking). The mechanical procedure: find the signs of v and a at the time in question; same sign ⟹ speeding up, opposite ⟹ slowing down.

On the spine particle at t = 3: v(3) = 3(1)(-1) = -3 < 0 while a(3) = 0 — the test is silent exactly at acceleration zeros. Check a neighborhood instead: just after t = 3, a > 0 with v < 0 (opposite signs), so the particle is slowing there. At t = 5: v(5) = 3(3)(1) = 9 > 0, a(5) = 12 > 0: speeding up. Always evaluate BOTH functions; the comparison is the answer.

Graph-reading version: given the GRAPH of v(t), speed increases where the graph moves AWAY from the t-axis (climbing while positive, or diving while negative) and decreases where it moves toward the axis. The away-from-axis reading answers speeding-up questions without computing a at all — a genuine exam shortcut when v is given graphically.
key_terms: sign(v) = sign(a) ⟹ speeding up; opposite signs ⟹ slowing down
On a v-graph, distance from the t-axis IS speed; moving away = speeding up
boxes: ap_alert

Full credit on 'speeding up at t = 5?' has three visible parts: v(5)'s value and sign, a(5)'s value and sign, and the comparison sentence. The exam awards the point for the COMPARISON, not the conclusion — show both signs even when the answer feels obvious.

sections.title: Displacement vs Total Distance
sections.subtitle: Net change versus odometer
sections.body:
Displacement over [t₁, t₂] is the net change in position: s(t₂) - s(t₁). Signed: a round trip has displacement zero. Total distance is the odometer reading — every leg counted positively — and requires breaking the interval at each direction change (each sign change of v), measuring each leg, and adding absolute values.

Spine particle on [0, 5]: positions s(0) = 0, s(2) = 20, s(4) = 16, s(5) = 20. Displacement: 20 - 0 = 20. Legs: 0→20 (distance 20), 20→16 (distance 4), 16→20 (distance 4). Total distance: 28. The two answers differ exactly because the particle backtracked on (2, 4); whenever v never changes sign, the two notions coincide.

The procedure formalized: (1) solve v = 0 on the interval and keep the sign CHANGES; (2) evaluate s at the interval's endpoints and every turning time; (3) displacement = last minus first; total distance = sum of |consecutive differences|. The turning-time evaluations are the step students skip — and the step every rubric prices.

Average velocity and average speed inherit the distinction: average velocity = displacement/time (here 20/5 = 4); average speed = total distance/time (28/5 = 5.6). Unit 2's average-rate machinery applies, with the same numerator subtlety. In Unit 8, integrals re-derive everything here — displacement as ∫v dt, distance as ∫|v| dt — so this chapter's bookkeeping becomes integration's setup.
key_terms: s(end) - s(start): net, signed, blind to backtracking
Sum of leg lengths between turning points: the odometer
Break at v's sign changes, evaluate s at every breakpoint and endpoint
boxes: ap_alert

Total distance from a position formula is a three-evaluation problem minimum: endpoints plus every turn. The most common error is summing |s(t₂) - s(t₁)| without breaking at turns — it silently computes |displacement| and loses the backtracking.

sections.title: Full Motion Analysis
sections.subtitle: The six-part FRQ, assembled
sections.body:
AP motion FRQs braid the chapter's threads into multi-part questions; here is the spine particle's complete dossier as a model. s(t) = t^3 - 9t^2 + 24t on [0, 6]: v = 3(t-2)(t-4), a = 6(t-3).

(1) At rest: t = 2, 4. (2) Moving left: v < 0 on (2, 4). (3) Direction changes: at both t = 2 and t = 4, since v's sign flips at each. (4) Speeding up: where v and a agree — a < 0 before t = 3 with v < 0 on (2,3): speeding up there; a > 0 after 3 with v > 0 after 4: also (4, 6). Slowing down on (0,2) and (3,4). (5) Displacement on [0,6]: s(6) = 36, s(0) = 0: 36. (6) Total distance: legs 0→20→16→36: 20 + 4 + 20 = 44.

Notice the infrastructure: ONE pair of sign charts (v and a on the same timeline) answers parts 1-4 without recomputation. Building the dual sign chart FIRST, before reading any sub-question, is the strongest exam strategy for motion problems — every answer becomes a lookup.

Vocabulary checklist to close the unit's core chapter — translate on sight: farthest right (maximize s, check critical times and endpoints), at rest (v = 0), changes direction (v sign flip), speeding up (signs agree), average velocity (displacement over time), total distance (odometer protocol). Six phrases, six procedures, no improvisation at test time.
key_terms: v and a signs on one timeline — the single artifact answering most motion sub-questions
Optimize s over critical times AND endpoints — a closed-interval check
Each motion phrase maps to one rehearsed procedure
boxes: ap_alert

Build the v/a dual sign chart in the first ninety seconds of any motion FRQ, before reading part (a). Parts (a) through (d) are almost always direct reads off the chart — the chart is the work; the answers are transcription.

mcq.question: A particle has position s(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t. On which interval is it moving left?
mcq.explanation: v = 3t^2 - 12t + 9 = 3(t-1)(t-3) < 0 between the roots: (1, 3).

mcq.question: v(2) = 6 and a(2) = -3. At t = 2 the particle is
mcq.explanation: Signs oppose (v > 0, a < 0): the acceleration is braking the rightward motion.

mcq.question: A particle's velocity is v(t) = (t - 3)^2. Which statement about t = 3 is true?

choices.A: The particle changes direction at t = 3
choices.B: The particle is at rest at t = 3 but does not change direction
choices.C: The particle is moving left at t = 3
choices.D: The particle's speed is maximal at t = 3

mcq.explanation: v(3) = 0 but v ≥ 0 on both sides — a pause without a sign change, so no turn. (Speed is minimal there, not maximal.)

mcq.question: s(t) = t^2 - 4t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 5. The total distance traveled is
Given the graph of v(t) is positive and decreasing on (0, 4), the particle on that interval is
mcq.explanation: v > 0: rightward. The graph approaches the t-axis (decreasing while positive): speed is dropping.

frq.question:
A particle moves along the x-axis with position s(t) = t^3 - 12t^2 + 36t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 8.
(a) Find all times the particle is at rest.
(b) Determine the time intervals on which the particle moves right and moves left, with justification from a sign chart.
(c) Find the displacement and the total distance traveled over [0, 8].
rubric: (b) v > 0 on (0,2) and (6,8) (right); v < 0 on (2,6) (left) — signs justified
Total distance: 32 + 32 + 32 = 96
frq.model_answer: (a) v(t) = 3t^2 - 24t + 36 = 3(t - 2)(t - 6); at rest at t = 2 and t = 6. (b) Sign chart for v: on (0,2), both factors give positive product — moving right; on (2,6), v < 0 — moving left; on (6,8), v > 0 — right again. (c) s(0) = 0, s(2) = 8 - 48 + 72 = 32, s(6) = 216 - 432 + 216 = 0, s(8) = 512 - 768 + 288 = 32. Displacement: s(8) - s(0) = 32. Legs: 0→32 (32), 32→0 (32), 0→32 (32): total distance 96.

frq.question:
A particle's velocity is v(t) = t^2 - 4t + 3 with acceleration a(t) = 2t - 4, for t ≥ 0.
(a) Find when the particle is at rest.
(b) Determine all intervals on which the particle is slowing down, using a dual sign analysis of v and a.
(c) The particle's position satisfies s(1) = 5. Using the tangent-line idea, estimate s(1.1), and state whether v's behavior near t = 1 makes this an over- or underestimate.
rubric: Since v(1) = 0 and v < 0 just after 1, the true position dips below 5: the estimate is an overestimate
frq.model_answer: (a) v(t) = (t - 1)(t - 3) = 0 at t = 1 and t = 3. (b) Signs: v > 0 on (0,1) and (3,∞); v < 0 on (1,3). a = 2t - 4: negative before 2, positive after. Slowing down where signs oppose: (0,1) (v>0, a<0) and (2,3) (v<0, a>0). (c) s(1.1) ≈ s(1) + v(1)·(0.1) = 5 + 0·(0.1) = 5. Just after t = 1 the velocity turns negative (the particle starts moving left), so the true s(1.1) is slightly less than 5 — the tangent estimate is an overestimate.

frq.question:
Two particles move on the same line: A with position x(t) = t^2 - 6t and B with position y(t) = 2t - 12, for t ≥ 0.
(a) At what time(s) do the particles occupy the same position?
(b) At what time do they have the same velocity, and what is each particle doing (direction, speeding up/slowing down) at that moment?
(c) Particle A is farthest left at what time, and what is its position there? Justify.
rubric: (b) x' = 2t - 6 = 2 = y' at t = 4; A: v = 2 > 0 right, a = 2 > 0 speeding up; B: constant velocity 2, neither
(c) x' = 0 at t = 3, x changes from decreasing to increasing (v: − to +)
Farthest left at t = 3, position x(3) = -9
frq.model_answer: (a) Set t^2 - 6t = 2t - 12: t^2 - 8t + 12 = (t - 2)(t - 6) = 0 — they meet at t = 2 and t = 6. (b) Velocities: x'(t) = 2t - 6 and y'(t) = 2. Equal when 2t - 6 = 2: t = 4. There, A has v = 2 > 0 (moving right) and a = 2 > 0 — same signs, speeding up. B moves right at constant speed 2 — neither speeding up nor slowing down (a = 0). (c) A's velocity 2t - 6 is negative before t = 3 and positive after: A moves left, turns at t = 3, then moves right — so its leftmost position is x(3) = 9 - 18 = -9.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: Derivatives don't care whether the input is time: marginal cost differentiates with respect to quantity, reaction rates with respect to concentration, and the AP rotates contexts deliberately. Master the structure once and every costume looks the same.
learning_objectives: Apply rate-of-change analysis to non-motion contexts: economics, biology, physics
Interpret marginal cost, revenue, and profit as derivatives
Analyze rates with non-time inputs and construct their units
Combine two related quantities through chain-rule rate composition
Determine when applied quantities are increasing, decreasing, or at extremes

sections.title: Marginal Thinking
sections.subtitle: Economics differentiates
sections.body:
Economics names its derivatives 'marginal': marginal cost is C'(q), the rate cost changes per unit of production; marginal revenue R'(q); marginal profit P'(q). The defining approximation: C'(q) ≈ the cost of producing one more unit beyond q. The derivative converts 'what does the NEXT one cost?' into calculus.

Why the approximation works: with Δq = 1, the tangent estimate ΔC ≈ C'(q)·Δq becomes ΔC ≈ C'(q). One unit is 'small' when production runs in the hundreds — the exam expects the ≈ and accepts the language 'approximately the cost of the (q+1)st unit.'

Profit structure: P(q) = R(q) - C(q), so P'(q) = R'(q) - C'(q). Profit rises while marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost and peaks where they EQUAL — the famous MR = MC condition is nothing but P' = 0, Unit 5's critical point condition arriving early in applied clothes. A firm producing where MR > MC should expand; where MR < MC, contract.

Typical cost curves decelerate then accelerate: C' falls at first (bulk efficiencies) and rises later (overtime, strained capacity) — language that translates to C'' < 0 then C'' > 0. Reading prose like 'costs rise at an increasing rate' into second-derivative signs is the chapter's recurring translation drill.
key_terms: C'(q): rate of cost per unit, ≈ cost of the next unit
P' = R' - C' = 0 — profit's critical point condition in economic dress
First derivative positive AND second derivative positive
boxes: ap_alert

'Marginal' on the AP simply means 'derivative of' — no economics background required. Marginal revenue at q = 50 is R'(50), interpreted with the standard four-ingredient sentence: at 50 units, revenue is increasing at about $[value] per additional unit.

sections.title: Non-Time Inputs
sections.subtitle: dV/dr and friends
sections.body:
Nothing in differentiation privileges time. A sphere's volume V(r) = (4/3)πr^3 has dV/dr = 4πr^2 — the rate volume changes per unit of RADIUS, units of cubic meters per meter. At r = 3, dV/dr = 36π: growing the radius from 3 by a small ε adds about 36πε of volume.

Notice the geometric punchline: dV/dr equals the sphere's surface area. Growing a sphere adds a thin shell whose volume is (surface area)·(thickness) — the derivative result is the geometry made algebra. The same phenomenon: dA/dr for a circle is 2πr, the circumference. These coincidences reward the students who pause to interpret.

Other standard non-time rates: dP/dV in physics (pressure per volume change), dC/dh for a cone filling (cross-sectional area appears), reaction rate d[product]/d[reactant] in chemistry. The mathematics is identical; only the interpretation sentence's nouns rotate. Units remain output-per-input, mechanically.

Evaluation questions often pair a non-time rate with a tangent estimate: 'by approximately how much does the volume increase as r goes from 3 to 3.02?' — ΔV ≈ (36π)(0.02) = 0.72π. The chapter-one machinery, with radii instead of clocks. Spot the structure and the costume dissolves.
key_terms: dV/dr, dP/dV — any input differentiates; units still output-per-input
dV/dr = surface area: growth happens in a thin boundary layer
Contexts rotate; the four-ingredient sentence and tangent estimate do not
boxes: ap_alert
When the input isn't time, do NOT write 'per second' by reflex. dV/dr at r = 3 carries cm³ per cm. Reflexive time-units in a radius problem is a real and avoidable rubric deduction.

sections.title: Chained Rates
sections.subtitle: Two relationships, one composition
sections.body:
Applied systems often chain: cost depends on gallons, gallons depend on time — so cost depends on time through the composition, and dC/dt = (dC/dg)(dg/dt). The chain rule, which Unit 3 built for compositions, IS the calculus of cascading dependencies; this section is its word-problem face.

Worked: a balloon's radius grows at dr/dt = 2 cm/s. How fast is volume growing when r = 5? V = (4/3)πr^3 depends on t THROUGH r: dV/dt = (dV/dr)(dr/dt) = 4πr^2 · 2 = 8πr^2. At r = 5: 200π cm³/s. The structure — differentiate the geometric relation, multiply by the given rate, evaluate at the moment — is precisely next chapter's related-rates method in its simplest, single-chain form.

Units audit the chain: (cm³/cm)·(cm/s) = cm³/s. ✓ Whenever a chained-rate answer's units fail to telescope correctly, a factor is missing — the audit catches dropped fees before the grader does.

Reading chains from prose: 'the price of electricity rises with demand, and demand rises through the afternoon' sets up dPrice/dt = (dPrice/dDemand)(dDemand/dt). Diagramming the dependency arrows (t → demand → price) before computing keeps multi-stage problems organized — and matches the layer-list habit from chain rule mastery, because it is the same skill.
key_terms: x → u → y: dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx) in applied costume
Chained units must cancel interior variables: (cm³/cm)(cm/s) = cm³/s
Arrow-sketch of which variable feeds which — the word problem's layer list
boxes: ap_alert

Single-chain rate problems ('radius grows at 2 cm/s; how fast does volume grow when r = 5?') are related rates with training wheels — differentiate the formula with respect to the intermediate variable, multiply by the given rate, substitute. The full method next chapter just adds implicit differentiation.

sections.title: Reading Applied Behavior
sections.subtitle: Signs, extremes, and sentences
sections.body:
Applied questions about behavior reduce to sign analysis of derivatives, exactly like motion. A drug's concentration K(t) rises while K' > 0, peaks where K' = 0 with a sign change, declines while K' < 0. 'When is the concentration greatest?' is a critical-point question; 'is the concentration rising or falling at t = 4?' is a single sign check. Motion's machinery, renamed.

The second derivative layers on: K'' < 0 while K' > 0 means concentration is 'rising at a decreasing rate' — absorption is slowing even though levels still climb. These mixed-sign descriptions are the AP's favorite applied prose, and they decode to sign pairs: 'rising at a decreasing rate' is f' > 0 with f'' < 0. But decode magnitude language carefully: 'decreasing at an increasing rate' means falling ever faster — f' < 0 with |f'| growing, which forces f'' < 0. Magnitude phrases route through |f'|, not through f'' alone.

That last subtlety is worth slowing for: 'decreasing at an increasing RATE' is ambiguous English that the AP resolves by magnitude — the decline is steepening, f'' < 0. When prose confuses, translate to a tiny sketch: draw the curve the sentence describes, read the signs off the sketch. Sketches disambiguate faster than grammar.

Closing synthesis: every applied rate question is one of five asks — value, rate, units, behavior (signs), or estimate (tangent). Identify the ask, run the matching procedure, write the four-ingredient sentence when interpretation is requested. Five asks, five procedures: the unit's entire applied surface, indexed.
key_terms: Rising/falling/peaked = sign analysis of the first derivative
'Rising at a decreasing rate' = f' > 0, f'' < 0 — decode as a sign pair
'Decreasing at an increasing rate': |f'| grows while f' < 0, so f'' < 0
boxes: ap_alert

When prose rate-language turns ambiguous, sketch the four template curves (rising-steepening, rising-flattening, falling-steepening, falling-flattening) and match the sentence to a picture. The sketch-match is faster and safer than parsing English under time pressure.

mcq.question: C(q) = 0.01q^2 + 4q + 900 dollars for q units. The marginal cost at q = 100 is
mcq.explanation: C'(q) = 0.02q + 4; C'(100) = 2 + 4 = 6 dollars per unit. (B evaluates C, not C'.)

mcq.question: A circle's area A = πr^2. The rate of change of area with respect to radius at r = 4 is
mcq.explanation: dA/dr = 2πr = 8π — the circumference at that radius, units of area per unit length.

mcq.question: Oil drains so that the volume satisfies dV/dh = 12 m³ per meter of depth, and the depth falls at dh/dt = -0.5 m/min. The volume is changing at
mcq.explanation: Chain: dV/dt = (dV/dh)(dh/dt) = 12 × (-0.5) = -6 m³/min — draining at 6 cubic meters per minute.

mcq.question: A population satisfies P'(t) > 0 and P''(t) < 0 for all t in (0, 10). The population is
mcq.explanation: Positive first derivative: growing. Negative second: the growth rate itself is shrinking — climbing but flattening.

mcq.question: Revenue is R(q) and cost is C(q). Profit is maximized (interior critical point) where
mcq.explanation: P' = R' - C' = 0 exactly when marginal revenue equals marginal cost. (A is break-even, a different concept.)

frq.question:
A company's revenue from selling q hundred phone chargers is R(q) = 60q - q^2 thousand dollars, and its cost is C(q) = 10q + 56 thousand dollars, for 0 ≤ q ≤ 30.
(a) Find the marginal revenue and marginal cost functions, and interpret R'(10) in a sentence.
(b) Write the profit function P(q) and find the production level where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
(c) Verify that the level in (b) gives a greater profit than producing nothing, by direct evaluation.
rubric: (a) R' = 60 - 2q, C' = 10; R'(10) = 40: at 1000 chargers, revenue rises ≈ $40 thousand per additional hundred
Comparison stated: 569 > -56, so q = 25 is better than shutdown
frq.model_answer: (a) R'(q) = 60 - 2q and C'(q) = 10 (thousand dollars per hundred chargers). R'(10) = 40: when the company sells 1,000 chargers, revenue is increasing at approximately 40 thousand dollars per additional hundred chargers. (b) P(q) = R - C = -q^2 + 50q - 56. Setting R' = C': 60 - 2q = 10, so q = 25 (2,500 chargers). (c) P(25) = -625 + 1250 - 56 = 569 thousand dollars, versus P(0) = -56 (a loss from fixed costs). Producing at q = 25 yields far greater profit than shutting down.

frq.question:
A spherical balloon is inflated so its radius grows at a constant 0.5 cm/s. Recall V = (4/3)πr^3.
(a) Find dV/dt as a function of r.
(b) Compute the inflation rate dV/dt at r = 6 cm, with units.
(c) Explain, using the shell interpretation of dV/dr, why dV/dt grows as the balloon expands even though dr/dt is constant.
rubric: (b) At r = 6: 72π cm³/s
(c) dV/dr = 4πr^2 is the surface area; each radius increment adds a shell of that area
Bigger balloon ⟹ bigger shell per cm of radius ⟹ faster volume growth at the same dr/dt
frq.model_answer: (a) dV/dt = (dV/dr)(dr/dt) = 4πr^2(0.5) = 2πr^2 cm³/s. (b) At r = 6: 2π(36) = 72π ≈ 226.2 cm³/s. (c) dV/dr = 4πr^2 is exactly the sphere's surface area: growing the radius by dr adds a thin shell of volume (area)(dr). As the balloon expands, that surface grows like r², so each half-centimeter of radius costs ever more volume — the volume rate climbs even at constant radius speed.

frq.question:
The concentration of a medication in the bloodstream is K(t) mg/L at t hours, with K'(t) > 0 on (0, 2), K'(2) = 0, K'(t) < 0 on (2, 12), and K''(t) > 0 on (5, 12).
(a) At what time is the concentration greatest? Justify.
(b) Describe the behavior of the concentration on (5, 12) in a sentence of the form 'decreasing at a(n) ___ rate,' and justify with the sign pair.
(c) The patient may take a second dose when the concentration's rate of decline slows to under 0.1 mg/L per hour in magnitude. Express this condition using K'.
rubric: (a) t = 2: K' changes from + to −, so K has its maximum there
(b) On (5,12): K' < 0 and K'' > 0 — K' rising toward zero, decline slowing: 'decreasing at a decreasing rate'
(c) Condition: |K'(t)| < 0.1, equivalently -0.1 < K'(t) < 0
Sign-pair justification explicit
frq.model_answer: (a) K' is positive before t = 2 and negative after, so the concentration rises, peaks, then falls: the maximum is at t = 2 hours. (b) On (5, 12), K' < 0 (falling) while K'' > 0 (K' is increasing toward zero — the decline is flattening). The concentration is decreasing at a decreasing rate. (c) The decline's magnitude is |K'(t)|; the condition is |K'(t)| < 0.1 mg/L per hour — that is, -0.1 < K'(t) < 0.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: Related Rates — Setting Up the Problem
hook: A ladder slides down a wall. The top falls, the bottom slides out, and the two rates are chained together by the Pythagorean theorem. Related rates problems are 80% setup — and the setup is a checklist you can learn cold before touching a single hard problem.
learning_objectives: Identify the variables, known rates, and requested rate in a word problem
Write the static equation relating the variables before differentiating
Differentiate the relation implicitly with respect to time
Substitute the snapshot values only after differentiating
Avoid the cardinal error: freezing a variable before the differentiation step

sections.title: The Anatomy of a Related Rates Problem
sections.subtitle: Variables changing together through time
sections.body:
Every related rates problem has the same skeleton: several quantities change with time; they are bound by a geometric or physical relationship; some of their rates are known; one rate is requested at a specific moment. The ladder: the wall height y and floor distance x both change; x^2 + y^2 = 25 binds them (a 5 m ladder); dx/dt is given; dy/dt is wanted at a snapshot.

The deep idea: differentiate the BINDING EQUATION implicitly with respect to t. Every variable is secretly a function of time, so x^2 + y^2 = 25 differentiates to 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt) = 0 — Unit 3's implicit machinery with t as the independent variable. Each variable emits its own rate as a fee; the static relation between quantities becomes a dynamic relation between rates.

Vocabulary for the chapter: the EQUATION is the timeless relationship (Pythagoras, similar triangles, volume formulas); the SNAPSHOT is the specific instant's data (x = 3 when we ask); the RATES are the dx/dt-type quantities, known and unknown. Keeping the three categories separate is most of the discipline.

Sign conventions ride on definitions: if x is the distance from the wall and the ladder slides OUT, dx/dt > 0; the top falling means dy/dt < 0. Define each variable so its meaning is unambiguous, and let the signs report direction honestly — a negative answer to 'how fast is the top moving' correctly says 'downward at that speed.'
key_terms: The timeless relation among variables (geometry/physics) — differentiated as a whole
The specific instant's values, used only after differentiating
Implicit differentiation in t: every variable emits its d/dt when touched
boxes: ap_alert

Related rates IS implicit differentiation with respect to t. Students who frame it that way reuse Unit 3's drilled mechanics; students who treat it as a new topic re-derive the method under pressure. It is not a new topic.

sections.title: The Five-Step Protocol
sections.subtitle: A checklist that survives panic
sections.body:
Step 1 — DRAW: sketch the situation, label every changing quantity with a VARIABLE (never a number if it changes), mark constants as numbers. Step 2 — LIST: write the known rates (with signs) and the requested rate, each in Leibniz notation. Step 3 — RELATE: write the equation binding the variables; this is where geometry enters. Step 4 — DIFFERENTIATE: implicitly, with respect to t, before any snapshot numbers touch the equation. Step 5 — SUBSTITUTE & SOLVE: now plug the snapshot in and solve for the requested rate.

The ladder, by protocol. Draw: right triangle, wall y, floor x, ladder 5 (constant — it is a number). List: dx/dt = 0.4 m/s (sliding out), find dy/dt when x = 3. Relate: x^2 + y^2 = 25. Differentiate: 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt) = 0. Substitute: at x = 3, y = 4 (Pythagoras fills the snapshot's gaps); 2(3)(0.4) + 2(4)(dy/dt) = 0, so dy/dt = -0.3 m/s. The top descends at 0.3 m/s.

Notice the snapshot completion move: y wasn't given at the moment, but the binding equation yields it (y = √(25 - 9) = 4). Step 5 routinely includes one such mini-solve — the static equation serves twice, once for differentiating and once for filling in the instant's missing values.

The protocol's order is load-bearing, and the next section explains the catastrophic error that violating it causes. For now: the checklist is five lines on your scratch paper, and FRQ graders can follow five labeled lines — the protocol IS the rubric map.
key_terms: Draw, List, Relate, Differentiate, Substitute — in that order, always
Changing quantities get letters; fixed quantities get numbers at the drawing stage
Use the binding equation to find the instant's missing values before solving
boxes: ap_alert

Write the known and requested rates in Leibniz notation as Step 2, every time: 'Given dx/dt = 0.4; find dy/dt when x = 3.' The two-line inventory forces the variable definitions and earns setup credit even if later algebra slips.

sections.title: The Cardinal Error
sections.subtitle: Never substitute before differentiating
sections.body:
The one mistake that destroys related rates problems: plugging snapshot values in BEFORE differentiating. Substitute x = 3 into x^2 + y^2 = 25 first and you get 9 + y^2 = 25 — differentiating that gives 2y(dy/dt) = 0, claiming the top never moves. The error froze x at the snapshot, deleting its rate from the universe.

The rule: anything that CHANGES stays a letter until after the differentiation step. Constants — the ladder's length, a cone's fixed shape ratio, a pole's height — may be numbers from the start, because their derivatives are genuinely zero. The classification question 'does this quantity change as time passes?' decides letter versus number at the drawing stage, and deciding it consciously is what the protocol's Step 1 is for.

The subtle version of the error involves DERIVED constants: in a cone with fixed shape, r/h stays constant (say r = h/3), and substituting r = h/3 into V = (1/3)πr^2h BEFORE differentiating is legal — because the relation r = h/3 holds for ALL time, not just the snapshot. The test: substitutions valid at every instant may happen early; substitutions true only at the snapshot must wait. 'Always true' versus 'true now' is the entire distinction.

Self-audit habit: after differentiating, scan your rate equation — every variable that changes should appear alongside its d/dt somewhere. A missing rate means a variable got frozen early. The audit takes five seconds and catches the error while it is still fixable.
key_terms: Substituting snapshot values before differentiating — freezes variables, deletes rates
Relations holding for all time (r = h/3 in a fixed cone) may be substituted early
Post-differentiation scan: every changing variable should carry its d/dt
boxes: ap_alert

The exam engineers problems where the cardinal error gives a clean-looking wrong answer (often 0 or a sign flip). If your related-rates answer is suspiciously tidy, audit for a frozen variable before trusting it.

sections.title: Geometric Equation Bank
sections.subtitle: Where Step 3 equations come from
sections.body:
Related rates problems draw their binding equations from a short, predictable bank. Pythagorean theorem: ladders, cars separating at right angles, kites, boats and docks — any right-triangle geometry. Similar triangles: shadows, cones of water, lamppost silhouettes — matching ratios like x/h = (x + s)/H. Volume formulas: spheres (4/3)πr^3, cylinders πr^2h, cones (1/3)πr^2h — tanks filling and draining. Trig relations: angles of elevation, rotating beacons — tan θ = opposite/adjacent leading to sec^2 θ dθ/dt terms.

Area and perimeter round out the bank: A = πr^2 for ripples, A = (1/2)bh for growing triangles, plus the occasional law of cosines for non-right triangles (BC-friendly). Memorizing the bank means Step 3 is recognition, not invention: read the geometry, pull the formula.

Multi-equation problems chain bank entries: a cone's water volume needs BOTH the cone volume formula AND a similar-triangles relation to eliminate one variable (substitute r = (R/H)h — an always-true relation — then differentiate the single-variable result). The elimination-then-differentiate pattern is the standard play for cone tanks, and it showcases the 'always true may substitute early' principle doing real work.

Next chapter runs the protocol at full speed across the bank's classic scenarios — ladders, cones, shadows, cameras. The setup discipline from this chapter is what makes those execution problems routine: with Draw-List-Relate-Differentiate-Substitute internalized, no scenario in the bank holds surprises.
key_terms: Pythagoras, similar triangles, volumes, trig ratios, areas — the Step 3 sources
Use always-true relations to reach one variable before differentiating (cone tanks)
Step 3 is pulling a known formula, not deriving new geometry
boxes: ap_alert

Cone tank problems: substitute the similar-triangles relation r = (R/H)h BEFORE differentiating (it is always true), reducing V to a function of h alone. Differentiating the two-variable form and juggling dr/dt is legal but doubles the work and the error surface.

mcq.question: x and y satisfy x^2 + y^2 = 100, with dx/dt = 3 when x = 6 and y = 8. Then dy/dt =
In a related rates problem, which quantity may be replaced by a number BEFORE differentiating?

choices.A: The ladder's distance from the wall at the snapshot
choices.B: The fixed length of the ladder
choices.C: The height on the wall at the snapshot
choices.D: Any quantity whose value is known

mcq.explanation: Only quantities constant for ALL time may be numbers early. Snapshot values (A, C) must wait until after differentiation — substituting them early freezes the variable.

mcq.question: A spherical snowball melts at dV/dt = -8 cm³/min. With V = (4/3)πr^3, the radius shrinks at r = 2 at rate dr/dt =
Water fills a cone-shaped tank (vertex down) with fixed proportions r = h/4. To find dh/dt from dV/dt, the most efficient setup is

choices.A: differentiate V = (1/3)πr^2h with both r and h as variables
choices.B: substitute r = h/4 first, then differentiate V = πh^3/48
choices.C: substitute the snapshot h-value first, then differentiate

mcq.explanation: r = h/4 is always true, so early substitution is legal and reduces to one variable. C is the cardinal error; A works but doubles the bookkeeping.

mcq.question: Two cars leave an intersection, one north at 30 mph, one east at 40 mph. The binding equation for the distance z between them is
mcq.explanation: Perpendicular directions make a right triangle: Pythagoras binds the three distances.

frq.question:
A 13-foot ladder leans against a wall. The base slides away from the wall at 2 ft/s.
(a) Define variables, state the given rate and the requested rate when the base is 5 feet from the wall, and write the binding equation.
(b) Find how fast the top of the ladder is sliding down the wall at that instant.
(c) A student substituted x = 5 into x^2 + y^2 = 169 before differentiating and concluded dy/dt = 0. Identify the error and explain why the conclusion is absurd physically.
rubric: (a) x = base distance, y = wall height; dx/dt = 2, find dy/dt when x = 5; x^2 + y^2 = 169
(b) 2x dx/dt + 2y dy/dt = 0; snapshot y = 12; 20 + 24 dy/dt = 0 → dy/dt = -5/6 ft/s
(c) Cardinal error: freezing x deleted dx/dt from the equation
Physical absurdity: a sliding base must move the top — the ladder is rigid
frq.model_answer: (a) Let x be the distance from wall to base and y the height of the top, both in feet, both functions of time. Given dx/dt = 2 ft/s; find dy/dt when x = 5. Binding equation: x^2 + y^2 = 169. (b) Differentiate: 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt) = 0. At x = 5: y = √(169 - 25) = 12. Then 2(5)(2) + 2(12)(dy/dt) = 0, so dy/dt = -20/24 = -5/6 ft/s — the top slides down at 5/6 ft/s. (c) Substituting x = 5 before differentiating freezes x as a constant, so its rate dx/dt vanishes from the differentiated equation, forcing dy/dt = 0. Physically absurd: the ladder is rigid — if the base moves, the top MUST move. Snapshot values may only enter after differentiation.

frq.question:
A conical tank (vertex down) has height 10 m and top radius 5 m. Water pours in at 3 m³/min.
(a) Use similar triangles to express the water's volume in terms of its depth h alone.
(b) Find how fast the depth is rising when h = 4 m.
(c) Explain why the depth rises more slowly when the water is deeper, referencing your differentiated equation.
rubric: (b) dV/dt = (πh^2/4) dh/dt; 3 = (π·16/4) dh/dt → dh/dt = 3/(4π) m/min
(c) Solves the rate equation for dh/dt = 4(dV/dt)/(πh^2), noting dh/dt is inversely proportional to h^2
Wider cross-section at greater depth: the same inflow spreads over more area, raising the level less
frq.model_answer: (a) The water cone is similar to the tank: r/h = 5/10, so r = h/2 — always true, so substitute now. V = (1/3)πr^2h = (1/3)π(h^2/4)h = πh^3/12. (b) Differentiate: dV/dt = (πh^2/4)(dh/dt). With dV/dt = 3 and h = 4: 3 = (π·16/4)(dh/dt) = 4π(dh/dt), so dh/dt = 3/(4π) ≈ 0.239 m/min. (c) Solving the rate equation: dh/dt = (4·dV/dt)/(πh^2) — inversely proportional to h². Deeper water means a wider surface (radius h/2), so the fixed 3 m³ per minute spreads across a larger disk and lifts the surface more slowly.

frq.question:
A street lamp is 6 m tall. A 1.5-meter-tall person walks away from the lamp at 1.2 m/s. Let x be the person's distance from the lamppost and s the length of their shadow.
(a) Use similar triangles to find the binding equation between x and s, and simplify it.
(b) How fast is the shadow lengthening?
(c) How fast is the TIP of the shadow moving away from the lamppost? Explain why this exceeds the walking speed.
rubric: (c) Tip position x + s = (4/3)x; d(x+s)/dt = (4/3)(1.2) = 1.6 m/s
Tip outruns the walker because the shadow lengthens while the person advances — both motions add
frq.model_answer: (a) The big triangle (lamp, tip) and small triangle (person, tip) are similar: 6/(x + s) = 1.5/s. Cross-multiplying: 6s = 1.5(x + s), so 4.5s = 1.5x and s = x/3. (b) Differentiate: ds/dt = (1/3)dx/dt = (1/3)(1.2) = 0.4 m/s. (c) The tip sits at distance x + s = x + x/3 = (4/3)x from the post, so its speed is (4/3)(1.2) = 1.6 m/s. The tip moves faster than the person because two effects stack: the person advances at 1.2 m/s AND the shadow simultaneously lengthens at 0.4 m/s — the tip carries both motions.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: Cones draining, shadows stretching, boats pulling away from docks, camera angles tracking rockets — the AP rotates through a repertory cast of related-rates scenarios. Meet each one once, slowly, and exam day becomes a reunion.
learning_objectives: Execute the five-step protocol fluently across the classic scenario bank
Solve right-triangle scenarios: ladders, separating vehicles, kites, and docks
Solve filling and draining problems for cones and cylinders
Solve angle-rate problems using trig relations and sec² fees
Diagnose which scenario archetype a novel problem belongs to

sections.title: Right-Triangle Scenarios
sections.subtitle: Pythagoras carries the load
sections.body:
The separating-vehicles classic: a car drives north at 60 km/h while another drives east at 80 km/h, both from the same intersection. How fast does the distance between them grow when the northbound car is 0.6 km and the eastbound 0.8 km from the start? Bind: z^2 = x^2 + y^2. Differentiate: 2z(dz/dt) = 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt). Snapshot: z = √(0.36 + 0.64) = 1. Substitute: dz/dt = (0.8·80 + 0.6·60)/1 = 100 km/h.

The boat-and-dock variant adds a twist: a rope from a dock pulley 1 m above the boat's bow is hauled in at 0.5 m/s. The rope length z and horizontal distance x satisfy z^2 = x^2 + 1, and the QUESTION is dx/dt while dz/dt is given. Differentiating and solving: dx/dt = (z/x)(dz/dt). Since z > x always (hypotenuse), the boat moves FASTER than the rope shortens — a counterintuitive conclusion the algebra delivers and the exam loves to probe conceptually.

Kites and balloons with an observer: altitude fixed or changing, horizontal drift given, find the rate the string pays out or the distance grows. All the same skeleton — identify which sides of the triangle change, which are constant (label numbers!), and differentiate Pythagoras.

The quiet workhorse: completing the snapshot with the binding equation (find z when x and y are known) before solving. In every right-triangle problem, that completion step is where dropped negatives and arithmetic slips concentrate — slow down exactly there.
key_terms: z² = x² + y² with both component rates feeding dz/dt
Given the hypotenuse rate, solve for a leg's rate: dx/dt = (z/x)dz/dt > dz/dt
Compute the triangle's missing side before substituting — the error hotspot
boxes: ap_alert

In separating-vehicle problems, the rates dx/dt and dy/dt are constant but dz/dt is NOT — it depends on the snapshot. A common conceptual MC question asks exactly this: 'is the separation rate constant?' No, and the differentiated equation shows why.

sections.title: Tanks, Cones, and Troughs
sections.subtitle: Volume scenarios and shape elimination
sections.body:
Cylindrical tanks are the gentle case: V = πR^2h with R constant, so dV/dt = πR^2(dh/dt) — the rates are proportional, and depth rises uniformly regardless of level. Any problem where the cross-section doesn't change with height behaves this way.

Cones are the featured act, and the previous chapter's eliminate-then-differentiate is the play: vertex-down cone of height H and rim radius R, water at depth h with surface radius r = (R/H)h (similar triangles, always true). V = (1/3)πr^2h = (πR^2/3H^2)h^3. Differentiate: dV/dt = (πR^2/H^2)h^2(dh/dt). The h^2 factor is why shallow water rises fast and deep water slowly — and why 'when the depth is 2' versus 'when the depth is 6' changes the answer by a factor of 9.

Troughs (prisms with triangular cross-section) run parallel: express the cross-section's area in terms of depth via similar triangles, multiply by the trough's length, differentiate. An isosceles-triangle trough 8 m long with top width 2 m and depth 1 m: at water depth h, surface width 2h, cross-section area h^2, volume 8h^2, so dV/dt = 16h(dh/dt).

Leaky variants superpose rates: water pours in at 3 m³/min while draining at 1 m³/min — the NET dV/dt = 2 enters the equation. When an FRQ says 'at the same time water drains at...', add the signed rates before substituting. Bookkeeping, not new calculus.
key_terms: Constant cross-section: dV/dt = (area)(dh/dt), level rises uniformly
After shape elimination, dV/dt ∝ h²(dh/dt) — depth dramatically changes rise rates
Inflow minus outflow gives the dV/dt that enters the equation
boxes: ap_alert

Trough problems hide their similar triangles in the CROSS-SECTION, not the 3D shape. Draw the 2D triangle face, relate surface width to depth there, then multiply by the prism's length. Students who try to find 3D similar solids stall; the geometry is flat.

sections.title: Angle Rates
sections.subtitle: Cameras, beacons, and sec² fees
sections.body:
Angle problems bind an angle to lengths through a trig ratio, and the differentiation fee is the trig derivative. The rising-balloon camera: a camera 100 m from a launch pad tracks a balloon rising at 4 m/s. With θ the elevation angle and h the height, tan θ = h/100. Differentiate: sec^2(θ)(dθ/dt) = (dh/dt)/100. At h = 100: θ = π/4, sec^2 θ = 2, so dθ/dt = 4/(100·2) = 0.02 rad/s.

The snapshot completion here computes sec^2 θ from the triangle: at h = 100, the hypotenuse is 100√2, so sec θ = √2 — or simply sec^2 θ = 1 + tan^2 θ = 1 + 1 = 2. The identity route avoids square roots entirely and is the recommended habit: sec^2 θ = 1 + (h/100)^2 turns every camera problem into algebra.

Rotating-beacon problems invert the given and requested: a lighthouse beam rotates at dθ/dt = 2 rev/min (convert: 4π rad/min!) and the question asks how fast the light spot races along a straight shore — tan θ = x/d differentiated gives dx/dt = d·sec^2(θ)(dθ/dt), exploding as the beam swings parallel to the shore. UNIT CONVERSION is the silent killer: revolutions to radians, degrees to radians — trig derivative formulas demand radians, full stop.

Which trig ratio to pick: tan for opposite/adjacent setups (heights vs ground distance — the majority), sin or cos when the hypotenuse is one of the changing or known quantities. Choosing the ratio whose ingredients you KNOW spares conversions later; choosing badly costs an extra identity pass but is never fatal.
key_terms: Height over ground distance: sec²θ dθ/dt = (dh/dt)/d — the camera template
sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ converts snapshot geometry to algebra, no roots
Angle rates must be in radians per time; convert revs and degrees first
boxes: ap_alert

Angle-rate answers carry units of RADIANS per time, and the exam checks: a beacon at '2 revolutions per minute' must become 4π rad/min before differentiated equations see it. The rev-to-rad conversion is worth a full point and is forgotten weekly in every classroom.

sections.title: Scenario Diagnosis
sections.subtitle: Mapping novel problems to the bank
sections.body:
Exam problems disguise the archetypes with fresh stories — but the diagnosis questions are fixed. What quantities change? (List them; they get letters.) What binds them? (Distances at right angles → Pythagoras; a shape's dimensions → volume formula plus similar triangles; an angle sighting → trig ratio.) What is given and what is asked? (Rates, with signs.) Three questions classify any problem into the bank.

Mixed archetypes occur: a fish on a line involves the reel rate (rope-haul) AND the rod-tip angle (angle rate); a draining conical coffee filter dripping into a cylindrical cup chains two volume scenarios with a shared dV/dt. Decompose into stages, solve the known stage, feed its output to the next — dependency diagrams from the chained-rates section scale up naturally.

What stays constant deserves explicit certification: 'the ladder is rigid' (length constant), 'the cone's shape is fixed' (ratio constant), 'the camera is mounted' (distance constant). Constants license number-labels at the drawing step, and stating them ('since the ladder's length is fixed at 13...') is rubric-visible justification.

A closing drill for self-test: write the binding equation ONLY — no differentiation — for five prompts: two ships separating at an angle (law of cosines), a snowball melting (sphere volume), a sliding ladder's ANGLE with the ground (cos θ = x/13), water in a trough (area times length), a shadow's tip (similar triangles). Five correct equations in five minutes means the diagnostic layer is solid, and execution is just the protocol.
key_terms: What changes? What binds them? What's given/asked?
Mixed problems split at shared quantities; solve and feed forward
Naming what is fixed (and why) earns justification credit and prevents letter/number errors
boxes: ap_alert

If a related-rates FRQ feels unfamiliar, classify before computing: right triangle, volume, or angle? The 30-second classification nearly always lands the problem in the bank, converting panic into protocol.

mcq.explanation: V = πh³/27, dV/dt = (πh²/9)dh/dt: 9 = (π·36/9)dh/dt = 4π dh/dt → dh/dt = 9/(4π).

mcq.question: A camera 50 m from a launch pad tracks a rocket rising at 30 m/s. When the rocket is 50 m high, the elevation angle increases at
